title: Priorities
summary: Work the problem in order: air, shelter, water, food. If you’re lost, STOP: Sit down, Think, Observe, Plan.

blocks.p: A rough guide, not an exact limit: a person can survive about 3 minutes in unsafe air, about 3 hours at a dangerous temperature, about 3 days without water and about 3 weeks without food. Work the problem in that order.

If you’re lost, STOP: Sit down and stay calm, Think, Observe, Plan. Then stay put: moving makes it harder for searchers to find you. Move only if your life is under immediate threat. Before any trip, leave word with someone about where you’re going and when you’ll be back, so a search starts in the right place.

list: Hypothermia can kill above freezing. Most cases happen between 30 and 50°F, and wind and wet clothes chill you fast. Get out of wind and rain early, before you’re soaked.
Treat all water from streams, ponds and lakes before drinking.
Burn dead and down wood. On New York state land, cutting standing trees is prohibited.
Check your whole body for ticks after time in the woods: under the arms, in and around the ears, belly button, backs of the knees, hair, between the legs and around the waist.
Remember COLD: keep clothing Clean, avoid Overheating (take layers off before hard work so sweat doesn’t soak them), wear it Loose and in layers, and keep it Dry.
Eat and drink regularly. Your body needs fuel to make heat.
Don’t eat snow or ice: it lowers your body temperature. Melt it, then treat it like any other wild water.

Never use a charcoal grill, lantern or portable camping stove inside a tent or snow shelter, and never use fuel-burning heaters or lanterns while sleeping in one. Carbon monoxide kills people every year this way.
Wear sunglasses, or cut thin horizontal slits in bark or cloth, to prevent snow blindness.
Never drink seawater. It can kill you: you dehydrate even as you get thirstier.
Collect rain and dew. On a beach, dig a hole behind the first group of sand dunes, deep enough to reach the water table, and treat what collects.

Only eat clams and mussels with unbroken shells that close when tapped, and throw out any that don’t open in cooking. Never take shellfish from an area closed to shellfishing or during a red tide: cooking does not destroy the toxin, and the water may look normal.
Check a tide chart before you go out. The rising tide can trap you, for example on a land bridge out to an island; at Acadia in Maine the tide range reaches about 12 ft.
Cover up. Water and sand reflect the sun and increase your chance of sunburn.

sources.used: STOP: Sit down, Think, Observe, Plan; hypothermia can kill above freezing; leave word with someone about your whereabouts and expected time of return

sources.name: National Park Service, Outdoor Emergency Plan
sources.used: If lost, stay put (moving makes you harder to find); move only if life is under immediate threat; leave a trip plan with a trusted contact

sources.name: Alaska State Parks (Alaska DNR), Hypothermia
sources.used: Most cases occur between 30 and 50°F; wind and wet clothes chill even in summer; remove layers when you start to sweat

sources.name: US Forest Service, Hypothermia
sources.used: Hypothermia above 40°F; avoid wet clothes, find shelter from wind; drink fluids and eat, water and carbohydrates help make heat

sources.name: CDC, How to Find Clean Water in an Emergency
sources.used: Streams, rivers, ponds and lakes must be treated

sources.name: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation, State Land Camping Rules
sources.used: Cutting standing trees is prohibited; use only dead and down wood for fires

sources.name: CDC, Preventing Tick Bites
sources.used: Full body check after tick areas, and the body areas to check

sources.name: US Army, Fight the Freeze (army.mil, 2011)
sources.used: COLD: keep clothing Clean, avoid Overheating, wear clothing Loose and Layered, keep clothing Dry; applies to gloves, boots and headgear

sources.name: US Army FM 21-76-1, Survival, Evasion, and Recovery (1999), chapters V to VII
sources.used: Keep clothing clean and dry, loose and layered, remove layers before strenuous activity; hat; do not eat ice or snow (lowers body temperature), melt it; sunglasses in sun or snow, slits in webbing or bark

sources.name: US Army ATP 3-50.21, Survival (2018), chapter 3
sources.used: Snow and ice no purer than their source, melt and purify; beach well behind the first group of sand dunes, deep enough to hit the water table

sources.name: US Consumer Product Safety Commission, Portable Heaters & Camping Equipment
sources.used: Never use fuel-burning heaters or lanterns while sleeping in tents; people die every year from heaters, lanterns or stoves inside tents

sources.name: CDC, Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning Prevention
sources.used: Never use a charcoal grill, hibachi, lantern or portable camping stove inside a home, tent or camper

sources.name: NOAA National Ocean Service, Can humans drink seawater?
sources.used: Drinking seawater can be deadly; you die of dehydration even as you become thirstier

sources.name: FDA, Selecting and Serving Fresh and Frozen Seafood Safely
sources.used: Discard clams and mussels with cracked shells or that do not close when tapped; throw out ones that do not open in cooking

sources.name: Massachusetts Department of Public Health, Red Tide (Paralytic Shellfish Poisoning)
sources.used: Cooking does not destroy the red tide toxin; toxic levels without discolored water; never harvest from closed areas

sources.used: Consult a tide chart; Bar Island land bridge trap; tidal range about 12 feet
